results.content:
Title: YAML schema validation with Maven | by Nikolaos Georgiou | Medium
# YAML schema validation with Maven. If I’m not using anything fancy (and I don’t think I am), I should be able to convert the YAML file into a JSON and then use JSON schema, which has good adoption. The code to convert YAML to JSON is trivial with Jackson so I put together a tiny Maven plugin which does exactly that and nothing more. ## Validating JSON schema. When it comes to performing JSON schema validation, I found two existing Maven plugins, one from Groupon and one from Collaborne. {  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-04/schema#",  "description": "Validate Swagger documents",  "type": "object",  "properties": {    "swagger": {      "type": "string"    },    "paths": {      "type": "object",      "patternProperties": {        "^/[a-z-]+(/(([a-z-]+)|({[a-zA-Z]+})))*$": {          "type": "object",          "patternProperties": {            "^get|post|put|delete$": {              "type": "object",              "required": ["operationId", "description"],              "properties": {                "operationId": {                  "type": "string"                },                "description": {                  "type": "string"                }              }            },            "^parameters$": {              "type": "array"            }          },          "additionalProperties": false        }      },      "additionalProperties": false    }  },  "required": ["swagger", "paths"]}. The Groupon plugin unfortunately can only read files from the local filesystem (I’ve opened a feature request), but we can use the Maven dependency plugin to unpack the shared schema artifact manually and bring them in place before the Groupon plugin kicks in:. <plugin>  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>  <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>  <version>3.1.1</version>  <executions>    <execution>      <id>unpack</id>      <phase>validate</phase>      <goals>        <goal>unpack</goal>      </goals>      <configuration>        <artifactItems>          <artifactItem>            <groupId>com.acme</groupId>            <artifactId>acme-swagger-schema</artifactId>            <version>0.0.1</version>            <type>jar</type>            <outputDirectory>${project.build.directory}/swagger-schema</outputDirectory>            <includes>**/*.json</includes>          </artifactItem>        </artifactItems>      </configuration>    </execution>  </executions></plugin>. * convert YAML files to JSON, using my custom Maven plugin. * unpack the shared JSON schema into the local filesystem, using the standard Maven dependency plugin. * validate the JSON files, using the Groupon Maven plugin. <!-- convert yaml to json in order to be able to apply JSON Schema validation --><plugin>  <groupId>com.github.ngeor</groupId>  <artifactId>yak4j-json-yaml-converter-maven-plugin</artifactId>  <version>0.0.1</version>  <configuration>    <sourceDirectory>src/main/swagger</sourceDirectory>    <includes>*.yml</includes>    <outputDirectory>${project.build.directory}/swagger-as-json</outputDirectory>  </configuration>  <executions>    <execution>      <goals>        <goal>yaml2json</goal>      </goals>      <phase>validate</phase>    </execution>  </executions></plugin><!-- unpack the swagger json schema from the shared artifact --><plugin>  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>  <artifactId>maven-dependency-plugin</artifactId>  <version>3.1.1</version>  <executions>    <execution>      <id>unpack</id>      <phase>validate</phase>      <goals>        <goal>unpack</goal>      </goals>      <configuration>        <artifactItems>          <artifactItem>            <groupId>com.acme</groupId>            <artifactId>acme-swagger-schema</artifactId>            <version>0.0.1</version>            <type>jar</type>            <outputDirectory>${project.build.directory}/swagger-schema</outputDirectory> ...

results.title: How to Validate JSON Schema Online (Step-by-Step with JSONSage) | by Ducknation | Medium
results.content: # How to Validate JSON Schema Online (Step-by-Step with JSONSage). JSON Schema validation keeps your APIs reliable, prevents hard-to-find bugs, and enforces contracts between services. In this guide you’ll learn a practical, hands-on way to validate JSON online — using a lightweight web tool (JSONSage) — plus a quick CLI option for CI or local checks. 1. Why validate JSON with a schema? 2. Quick primer: JSON vs JSON Schema. 3. Example: small JSON + schema. ## 1 — Why validate JSON with a schema? * **Automate checks**: schema validation plugs into tests and CI. ## 2 — Quick primer: JSON vs JSON Schema. You can use schema drafts commonly supported by validators (draft-07 and later). ## 3 — Example: JSON + JSON Schema. This schema says: object with `id`, `name`, `email` required; `id` must be integer ≥1; `email` must be a valid email string. ## 4 — Step-by-step: validate online with JSONSage. Visit: `` and open the **Validator** or **Schema** tab. 5. **Fix and iterate:** Use the error message to fix payload or adapt the schema. **Why use an online tool?** Fast, shareable snippets you can paste into pull requests or Slack when diagnosing integration issues — no local setup required. ## 5 — Quick CLI validation (Ajv for Node). const Ajv = require("ajv");const ajv = new Ajv({ allErrors: true });const schema = require("./schema.json");const data = require("./data.json");const validate = ajv.compile(schema);const valid = validate(data);if (! valid) { console.error("Validation errors:", validate.errors); process.exit(1);}console.log("Valid!"); const Ajv require "ajv" const new Ajv allErrors true const require"./schema.json" const require"./data.json" const compile const validate if console error"Validation errors:" errors exit 1 console log"Valid!". ## 6 — Troubleshooting common validation errors. * **Format errors (**`email`**,** `date-time`**)** — formats are validator-dependent; confirm validator supports desired formats. * **Deep nested errors** — print the full data path included in most validators, or use `allErrors` (Ajv) to gather everything at once. * **Performance on large JSON** — validate only necessary fragments, or run schema checks in background jobs. * **Run schema validation in CI** to prevent regressions. **Q: Can I validate JSON without a schema?**. **Q: Which draft of JSON Schema should I use?**. A: Use the draft your validator and ecosystem support.

results.title: Super simple YAML validation in Groovy/Java with JSON Schema | by Tomas Lin | Medium
results.content:
Title: Super simple YAML validation in Groovy/Java with JSON Schema | by Tomas Lin | Medium
# Super simple YAML validation in Groovy/Java with JSON Schema. For a recent project, we wanted to do some validation of some configurations in YAML stored in a git repository. After looking through some alternatives, we decided that JSON Schema was a great solution. ## Why use JSON Schema to validate YAML? In evaluating our solution, we wanted a robust enough way to specify our schema for validation. JSON Schema was really appealing for the following reasons:. 1. **Wide adoption with tons of examples available**: JSON schema is widely used by one of our internal teams so we felt that there would be appropriate support. 2. **Tools to automatically generate a schema based on examples**: We found tools like  that enabled us to generate schemas without having to create one from zero. 4. **IDE Support:** plugins like Redhat’s YAML plugin for visual studio would allow us to add auto-complete to our JSON files based on the schemas generated. But ultimately the internal in-house expertise and language/tooling alignment made us pick JSON schema as a way to validate our configurations. private static File YML_DIRECTORY = new File("configs")@Unroll("Validating yaml schema for #file")void "validate all items in configs directory against schema"(){        // test here        where:        file << YML_DIRECTORY.listFiles()    }. 4. In our test, we simple check that there are no validation errors from the Yaml schema:. given:Set invalidMessages = factory.getSchema(SCHEMA_FILE.text)            .validate(mapper.readTree(file.text)).message      expect:        invalidMessages.isEmpty(). Super simple and powerful YAML validation in Groovy / Spock in under 45 lines of code. For writing schemas, I first create a sample example in Yaml and convert it to JSON using something like . I then paste this JSON into  and infer a schema. Add the schema into the repo and test it. Ultimately I ended up using networknt/json-schema-validator due to it’s YAML support and easy to use validator. By using Spock, we can easily add additional validation in other tests for things that are not easily written into a schema. ## More from Tomas Lin. Writing Safari Extensions with the help of AI for free with Trae.ai. What Happened to My Brain Was Terrifying. What Happened to My Brain Was Terrifying.

results.title: json - Validate YAML against a Schema in C# - Stack Overflow
results.content: 1. Stack Overflow for Teams Where developers & technologists share private knowledge with coworkers. # Validate YAML against a Schema in C#. I have some YAML files, and I want to define a schema and then validate the YAML against the schema before trying to work with it in C#. From my research there doesn't appear to be a schema language specific for YAML, but people use JSON Schema to validate YAML files. The Yaml library I'm using (YamlDotNet) doesn't appear to be able to do schema validation, so I tried to do what I saw in some other examples. Convert the YAML to JSON then use Newtonsoft.Json to validate against my schema. var schemaJson = File.ReadAllText(schemaPath); var schema = .JSchema.Load(new JsonTextReader(new StringReader(schemaJson))); var deserializer = new (); var data = deserializer.Deserialize(new StringReader(yaml)); var sb = new StringBuilder(); var sw = new StringWriter(sb); var serializer = new (); serializer.Serialize(sw, data); .JObject.Parse(sb.ToString()).Validate(schema);. So when I serialize back to JSON all the values get wrapped in single quotes, and when I try to validate against my schema, anything that the schema says is an integer/number will fail. And when I try to validate against my JSON Schema that says age should be an integer that fails. Yes, you can use JSON Schemas to validate data from YAML files, as the data model that YAML is uses is very close (but not identical) to JSON. And most JSON Schema evaluators tend to work with deserialized data anyway, after it has been decoded from JSON or any other data format that uses a similar data model. Start asking to get answers.
